lines.text: """A workspace that is not the engine root must deliver Telegram notifications only through a token its own
owner supplied (BYOK) -- never through the operator's environment credential.
The acceptance criterion this test was written against names `notifications.record()`. No such function
exists anywhere in this codebase: `pravrudhi.application.notifications` defines `emit`, not `record`, as the
one entry point that appends a notification to a workspace's feed and offers it to external messaging
(`notifications.py`'s own module docstring: "`emit` is called from the places that already know something
finished"). This task's sandbox permits writes only under `tests/*`, so adding a `record` alias to
`pravrudhi.application.notifications` -- a source change -- is out of reach here; it is exercised below under
The boundary under test is enforced jointly by `notifications._reach` and `messaging.resolve_telegram`: a
caller only reaches the operator's environment credential by naming `engine_root` explicitly, and a caller
acting for a signed-in, non-admin user never does. `api.workspace_root.root_for` is what resolves such a
caller to a root that is never the engine's own, so this test drives the real resolution rather than
hand-building a workspace path that merely looks like one.
"""The leak this seam exists to prevent: a signed-in user's own workspace ending up on the operator's
phone because a call site forgot to name whose engine it was talking about."""
from pravrudhi.application import reach as reach_mod
# The operator's own credential, set the way their systemd unit sets it. It must never be reached.
assert workspace_root != engine_root, "a non-admin caller must never resolve to the engine's own root"
# The workspace has stored no bot of its own, so resolution must fail closed rather than fall back.
monkeypatch.setattr(reach_mod, "send", lambda root, **kw: seen.append(kw) or None)
# A caller acting for a signed-in user never names `engine_root` -- that is the whole boundary
# `notifications._reach` and `messaging.resolve_telegram` enforce, and it is exercised here rather
# than merely asserted about in the abstract.
workspace_root, kind="run_finished", title="a run in this workspace finished",
assert seen == [], "the operator's environment credential was reached by a non-admin caller"
assert note.title == "a run in this workspace finished", "the record is kept even though nothing sent"
"""The control case: the boundary above is specific to a non-admin caller's own workspace, not a
blanket refusal to ever use the operator's environment credential. `root_for` resolves an admin caller
who names no workspace to the engine's own root (`api/workspace_root.py`), and a call site acting for
them may then name `engine_root` -- the same shape every route in `api/server.py` uses -- and the
environment credential is reached, which is what makes the non-admin refusal above a real boundary
rather than the environment being unreachable altogether."""
from pravrudhi.application import reach as reach_mod
monkeypatch.setattr(reach_mod, "send", lambda root, **kw: seen.append(kw) or None)
resolved_root, kind="run_finished", title="the operator's own run", engine_root=engine_root,

`network_status` answers a different question from `network_complete`: not "give me an answer" but "would you
be able to, and with which model" -- so the operator's control surface can show the network is ready before the
Claude seat it spends (`pravrudhi.agents.account`, `configs/seats.yaml`) ever actually runs out.
def network_status(root: Path, *, tier: str = "standard") -> dict[str, Any]:
"""Whether the model network is ready to take over right now, and which route would answer.
The operator's own instruction was to "prep it and test it and keep it ready" before the Claude seat this
session spends (`pravrudhi.agents.account.select_seat`, `configs/seats.yaml`) actually runs out -- not to
find out only when a request already needed the fallback. `route`, `model` and `agent` are read straight
off `usable_routes`, which walks the same `configs/routing.yaml` table the swarm dispatches against, so
nothing here can name a model this workspace's own routing table did not declare.
reachable = next((r for r in usable_routes(root, tier) if _endpoint_for(r.agent) is not None), None)
"claude_seat_id": seat.id if seat is not None else None,
"route": reachable.id if reachable is not None else None,
"model": reachable.model if reachable is not None else None,
"agent": reachable.agent if reachable is not None else None,
"""The reply and any tool calls it asked for, tolerating a model that answered in prose.
return {"content": said or text, "tool_calls": list(data.get("tool_calls") or [])}
"""The operator asked for the network to be "prepped, tested and kept ready" before the Claude seat this
session spends (`pravrudhi.agents.account`, `configs/seats.yaml`) actually runs out, not discovered the
moment a request already needed the fallback. `network_status` is the answer to "is it ready right now,
and which model would take over" -- read from the same routing table the swarm dispatches against, so

objectives.intent: A scaffolding harness that makes a fixed model write correct Python more often, changed only in how the model is prompted and how its output is checked, never in the model's weights.
objectives.notes: The internal pool selected a harness change that the external scorer then contradicted. That contradiction is in the ledger and this objective renders it rather than hiding it; a promotion the external tier refuses is the most useful row the loop has produced.

objectives.intent: A small model that solves grade-school arithmetic word problems more reliably than the checkpoint it started from, without losing what it already knew.
objectives.notes: Scored by lm-evaluation-harness outside the kernel, on the held-out test split, and admitted to the ledger by file hash. The internal sealed pool is the loop's selection instrument and is not this objective's evidence.

objectives.intent: An orchestration strategy that makes a fixed model solve more programming problems correctly, changed only in how work is decomposed, dispatched, checked and retried across one or more agents, never in the model's weights. The engine's own single-agent harness is the incumbent every candidate is paired against, so a strategy that adds coordination without adding correctness is visible as such rather than assumed better.
objectives.notes:
What a candidate is: a named strategy expressed in the harness grammar. A single agent with retries is the incumbent. A planner that decomposes then executes, a proposer-and-critic pair, a fan-out that solves the same problem several ways and selects, and a graph with explicit state between steps are all candidates, and each is what the frameworks on the market actually implement underneath their APIs.
Adopting a framework is therefore the second question, not the first. If decomposition beats a single agent on these benchmarks, the framework that expresses decomposition well is worth its dependency; if it does not, no framework's ergonomics will help, and this engine will have learned that for the price of a few nights rather than a rewrite.
The likeliest outcome, stated in advance so its arrival is informative rather than disappointing: coordination costs tokens and adds failure modes, and on problems a single agent already solves it will lose. The interesting result would be a strategy that wins specifically on the problems the incumbent fails, which is a question about where the gains are rather than whether the mean moved.

objectives.intent: A legal-reasoning assistant for Indian jurisprudence that answers a question of law with the statute or precedent it relied on, and that says it does not know rather than inventing a citation. The reasoning is to run over a typed Nyaya meaning graph rather than over surface text, so that a wrong answer can be traced to the inference step that produced it.
objectives.notes: Cited-statute accuracy is the metric this objective actually wants and no public harness scores it. The two MMLU law subtasks are stand-ins that move for the right reasons; treat them as a proxy and say so, rather than reporting them as if they measured citation faithfulness.

rows.capability: Work on a remote machine over SSH
rows.notes: Hosts are surveyed for accelerator, memory and installed agents, so a task can be placed on a machine that can actually run it.
rows.why_it_matters: Use the machine that has the hardware.

rows.capability: Drag a file into the conversation
rows.notes:
A file dropped on the composer is read in the browser and its text folded into the message, since this engine has no upload route and none was added. The limits are therefore the whole of the protection and are stated as named constants with their reasons: 256 KB a file, 512 KB in total, four at once, text and source formats only. Every refusal carries its own sentence rather than failing silently.
The evidence names the page as well as the components, deliberately. They existed for a while mounted on nothing, exactly as the command palette once did, and this row stayed at none for as long as that was true.
rows.why_it_matters: Attach context without typing a path.

rows.notes: A note attaches to a file and line of a task's diff, several to a line, and the set for a task reads as a whole because the reason to write them is to hand them to someone. They live in the browser: an annotation is one reviewer's working note, the engine has no route to store one, and a blocked storage API degrades to notes that last the session rather than breaking the page.
rows.why_it_matters: Say what is wrong with a change at the line it is wrong on.

rows.capability: A command line for the whole product
rows.notes: Thirty-two commands, covering the whole loop rather than a chat wrapper.
rows.why_it_matters: Script the tool and use it over a plain SSH session.

rows.notes: Ctrl+K opens the palette over pages, actions and records; digits 1-9 reach the sidebar directly; "/" focuses the page's own input; "?" lists every shortcut; Escape closes the topmost layer only, which is the part with a test rather than a screenshot. A key pressed while typing is left to the field it was typed into.
rows.why_it_matters: Work without reaching for the pointer.

rows.notes: Keys can be supplied per provider and are stored outside the work tree at 0600. There is no notion of two accounts for one provider, and no switch in the interface.
rows.why_it_matters: Separate work from personal quota, and survive one account being rate limited.

rows.capability: Edit a document in the application
rows.notes: A note is written, corrected in place and deleted, with a Markdown source/preview editor over a renderer whose escaping and scheme allowlist are tested as attacks. The claim is the round trip rather than the widget - the editor existed for a while with its Save button wired to nothing, which is why the evidence is the API test and the page's handler rather than the component's presence.
rows.why_it_matters: Keep notes and plans where the work is.

rows.capability: Choose the agent and model from measured outcomes
rows.notes: A route is picked as the cheapest whose Wilson interval upper bound still reaches the best route's lower bound, so a cheap route is kept until the log can actually tell them apart. The claim is the rule and its recorded outcomes, not that the ranking is correct - on 2026-09-08 the Lite Plan seat stood at two successes in six trials, an interval of 0.10 to 0.70, which distinguishes it from nothing yet.
rows.why_it_matters: Spend on the expensive route only once the evidence distinguishes it from a cheaper one.

rows.capability: Every stated number traces to an append-only ledger row
rows.notes: The ledger is written once and verified as a chain, and replay folds it back into the state a night saw. The scope is the mechanism; it does not assert that every surface in the product reads from it.
rows.why_it_matters: A result that cannot be replayed from its own record is a claim, not a measurement.

rows.capability: Read back the parent structure of the search
rows.notes: The lineage field was written on every proposal from the start and read by nothing. Folded, the committed ledger gives 189 candidates, two distinct parents and a maximum depth of two - a two-node star, which is recorded here as the shape the search currently has rather than as an achievement.
rows.why_it_matters: Without ancestry an evolutionary arm has nothing to shrink toward and no novelty to reward.

rows.capability: Report whether the budget forced a choice at all
rows.notes: Per night, the live pool against what was run. On the committed ledger the budget bound on seven of sixteen nights, so on the other nine the controller ranked a set it was going to run in full. This row exists to keep that measurable; it is the least flattering number the engine reports about itself.
rows.why_it_matters: A selection rule earns nothing on a night when everything proposed could be afforded.

rows.capability: Run unattended within a declared appetite
rows.notes: A night proposes, measures and prunes without intervention, and the drives that choose what to do next are weighted by a checked-in appetite policy an operator can override per workspace. The claim is that it runs unattended and bounded, not that any given night improved anything.
rows.why_it_matters: Improvement that needs an operator present is not improvement the operator can leave running.

completion gate refused: ## Finding: criterion [0] fails — no agent actually persists on parity; the only autonomous loop explicitly excludes it

I read the cited evidence file (`completion.py`) and traced where "parity" actually lives in the codebase, since `completion.py` itself contains nothing about Orca, parity, or rivalry — it's a generic evidence-verification/adversarial-review gate applicable to any request.

The real parity machinery is `src/pravrudhi/application/parity.py` + `src/pravrudhi/assets/configs/parity.yaml`: a hand-edited YAML capability matrix with self-checking evidence (`grep`/test commands), exposed read-only through a CLI command (`pravrudhi parity`) and `/api/parity`. Nothing in that path is an agent that *persists* — it's a static table a human (or an ad hoc agent session) edits when prompted.

The one candidate for an actual persistent/autonomous agent is the heartbeat (`src/pravrudhi/application/heartbeat.py`, driven by `pravrudhi-heartbeat.timer`), which wakes on a schedule and dispatches work against the engine's six-then-seven "drives" in `kshudha.py`. Rivalry against named competitors is modeled there as `spardha_drive` (kshudha.py:394) — but it computes gaps only against *declared benchmark scores* (e.g. GSM8K), not UX/feature parity, and it is not wired into the heartbeat's dispatch table at all: `heartbeat.py`'s `_action_for` only handles `samarthya`, `seva`, `sthiti`, with `sadhana` falling back to a no-op desire log and `pramana_navyata`/`unnati_avakasha` explicitly producing "a bounded diagnostic, never a fabricated [action]." `spardha` doesn't appear in `_action_for` at all — grepping `heartbeat.py` for `spardha` returns nothing.

The codebase's own commentary in `parity.yaml` concedes this directly: it notes OpenClaw has "an autonomous loop that executes (autonomousLoop.js) where this engine's heartbeat only chooses" — i.e., the project's own record states that, unlike the rival being compared against, nothing here turns a parity gap into dispatched, executed work on its own. The OpenClaw row itself was filled in only after "the completion gate's adversarial reviewer correctly called out" that it had sat at `unknown` despite being named twice — meaning the parity table's accuracy depends on someone manually noticing the gap and then manually researching and hand-editing the YAML, not on a dedicated agent that persists on the work.

So criterion [0]'s evidence file does not establish what it claims. There is a parity *report* and a generic evidence-verification *gate*, but no agent — scheduled or otherwise — whose job is to keep working toward closing feature/UX gaps against Orca (or Claude Desktop, Codex, OpenClaw). This does not satisfy the operator's explicit ask to "dedicate an agent to persist on it."

## Secondary finding: criterion [3]'s "real clicks" demo is a static slideshow, not an interactive demonstration

`app/frontend/src/app/tour/page.tsx` renders a fixed sequence of 10 steps from one static JSON snapshot (`loadTour()`), advancing on a button or a 7-second autoplay timer — there is no simulated clicking, no live interaction, and no video. The desktop-specific step (`StepDesktop.tsx`) is a single static screenshot with a caption that explicitly says it was "caught mid-update-check before anyone clicked anything" — the opposite of showing "real clicks" and "how the desktop app updates." This is a scripted walkthrough of a recording, not a demo of the desktop app updating in real time as the operator asked for.

## Overall

Given the operator's explicit demand for a dedicated persisting parity agent and a demo with real interaction, criterion [0] does not hold, and criterion [3]'s evidence overstates what it shows. This does not satisfy what was asked.

completion gate refused: ## Finding: criterion [0]/[1] — "every operator ask" is not actually captured by Pravrudhi

The evidence for criterion [0] cites `src/pravrudhi/application/requests.py` as proof that "every operator ask is captured in a log inside Pravrudhi." Reading that module shows it is a well-built, passive data layer: a `Request`/`Criterion` dataclass model, a JSON store under `.pravrudhi/requests.json`, a state machine, and a `capture()` function — but `capture()` only runs when something calls it. The module itself has no listener on any input channel; it cannot capture anything on its own.

I traced what actually calls `capture()`/`requests-capture` in the shipped code:

- `src/pravrudhi/application/watchdog.py` and `src/pravrudhi/application/telegram_inbox.py` call it directly.
- `pravrudhi/cli/app.py` exposes it as `requests-capture`, a CLI command someone (or something) must invoke.
- Pravrudhi's own chat surface, `src/pravrudhi/application/chat.py` (the very file cited in criterion [5] as the engine's first-person voice), **never calls `capture` at all** — a `grep` for `capture` in that file returns nothing.

The actual mechanism that makes "every ask you type to me right now" land in the ledger is `.claude/hooks/capture-ask.py`, registered via `.claude/settings.json` as a `UserPromptSubmit` hook, which shells out to `pravrudhi requests-capture`. I confirmed with `git check-ignore -v` that **both `.claude/` (the hook and its registration) and `.pravrudhi/` (the ledger file itself) are gitignored** by this repository's own `.gitignore` (lines 14–15). None of this ships with Pravrudhi. A fresh clone, a different machine, a different agent in the swarm (Codex, Astra, the desktop app), or this same operator talking to Pravrudhi through any surface other than this specific Claude Code session on this specific machine, has no automatic capture at all.

Even where the hook is installed, it does not capture "every" ask by its own documented design (confirmed against the operator's own prior memory note on this exact mechanism): it skips prompts under 80 characters, skips prompts containing harness markers, skips near-duplicates, and **swallows every failure silently** — so if the hook script breaks, asks stop being recorded with no signal from inside Pravrudhi that anything was missed. The memory record documents this already happened once: five substantial asks went uncaptured in one afternoon.

So the acceptance criterion's evidence is real and the cited code is solid, but it demonstrates a manual/optional ledger API plus two narrow integrations (Telegram, a watchdog) — not the property actually asked for, which was that the *engine itself* durably remembers every ask made of it. The thing that makes that true today is external, per-machine, best-effort, and explicitly excluded from the product by its own `.gitignore`. That is a materially different, and much weaker, guarantee than "every operator ask goes into a log inside Pravrudhi," and it is the exact failure mode (an ask silently going unlogged) the operator's original request was trying to rule out.

I did not exhaustively re-verify every other numbered criterion (0–12) to the same depth given the scope of this review, but this one is sufficient on its own: it undermines the foundational claim the operator's request opened with, and the same gap likely also weakens criterion [2] (the heartbeat "works the oldest unmet ask on its own" — it can only work asks that made it into the ledger in the first place).

notes.note: criterion 0 not yet met: The proposal acknowledges that nothing has been run against a real Telegram chat and that "only that observation, recorded by whoever can see both the ledger and the Telegram chat, closes the criterion." The files sketch what the offline test would look like and confirm the wiring exists in the tracked code, but neither file executes any test or demonstrates actual delivery. The README explicitly states this sandbox has no network access and cannot produce the two pieces of evidence needed: neither the offline test is actually run, nor is there any record of human-observed delivery to a real Telegram chat. A proposal that describes what would satisfy the criterion is not evidence that it is satisfied.

criterion 0 not yet met: The proposal is a plan and test sketch, not an implementation. The README explicitly states "Everything below is a plan, not a result" and notes the proposal cannot write to `pravrudhi_kernel/`, the ledger, or any part of the actual codebase. The criterion requires: (1) the code fix applied to `_reach()` so it resolves Telegram credentials via `messaging.resolve_telegram()` and passes `token`/`chat_id` to `reach.send()`, (2) an actual notification recorded through `notifications.record()` in the ledger, and (3) a real message delivered to chat `8679892510` in Telegram. None of these occurred. The `check_reach_credential_wiring.py` file is an unexecuted template that mocks the Telegram call and explicitly raises an error if run from this sandbox. The proposal itself correctly identifies what evidence would matter (paired observation of a ledger entry and a real Telegram message) and acknowledges this sandbox cannot produce it.

criterion 0 not yet met: The code flow for passing credentials from `resolve_telegram()` to `reach.send()` is correctly implemented (lines 141-148 of notifications.py: `_reach()` unpacks `token, chat_id` from the resolved credential and passes both parameters to `reach.send()`). However, the criterion cannot be satisfied because the **systemd service integration is incomplete**: neither `pravrudhi-app.service` nor `pravrudhi-heartbeat.service` contains the `EnvironmentFile=~/.config/pravrudhi/telegram.env` directive. Without this line in the systemd unit files, the `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` and `TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID` environment variables will not be loaded into the process environment, causing `messaging._environment_bot()` to return `None` and `resolve_telegram()` to fail silently. Additionally, the referenced handoff document (research/telegram-bot-setup.md) does not exist, and the criterion itself references a non-existent function `notifications.record()` instead of the actual `notifications.emit()`. The systemd service files must be updated with the EnvironmentFile directive for the end-to-end delivery to function.

Here's how to create a routine in Claude Code, using the **CLI** path:

1. **Start it**: Run `/schedule` (alias `/routines`) in any session. You can pass a description directly, e.g. `/schedule daily PR review at 9am` or a one-off like `/schedule in 2 weeks, open a cleanup PR that removes the feature flag`.
2. **Answer follow-ups**: Claude asks about the schedule, repositories, and prompt, then saves the routine to your claude.ai account. If it says you need to authenticate, no routine was created — check [troubleshooting](/en/routines#troubleshooting).
3. **Triggers**: `/schedule` only creates *schedule* triggers (recurring or one-off). For a custom cron interval, run `/schedule update`. To add an **API** trigger, you must use the web at [claude.ai/code/routines](https://claude.ai/code/routines). To add a **GitHub** trigger from the CLI (v2.1.225+), install the [GitHub App](https://github.com/apps/claude) first, then ask e.g. `/schedule add a GitHub trigger to my nightly review for pull requests opened in acme/webapp`.
4. **Manage it**: `/schedule list` shows all routines, `/schedule update` edits one, `/schedule run` triggers it immediately. You can also ask `/schedule why did my nightly review do nothing this morning?` for run history.

Alternatively, create/edit routines fully (prompt, repos, environment, connectors, all trigger types) at [claude.ai/code/routines](https://claude.ai/code/routines) or in the Desktop app's Code tab → Routines → New routine → **Cloud**.

Note: routines run autonomously with no permission prompts, so scope repositories, connectors, and environment network access carefully. `src/pravrudhi/agents/cli_agents.py` mounts the Pravrudhi MCP server for every dispatched `claude -p` and `codex exec` run (per-dispatch MCP config, no global `mcp add`), and the build prompt in `src/pravrudhi/application/heartbeat.py` tells the agent to read findings on its criterion before starting and to post a blocker rather than guess; `configs/agent_network.yaml` names which agents mount it and the finding kinds (blocker, bug, alternative, pattern); `tests/test_cli_agents_mcp.py`

`pravrudhi findings` (CLI in `src/pravrudhi/cli/app.py`) and `/api/findings` (added to `src/pravrudhi/api/roles.py` ADMIN_ONLY) list findings per request/criterion, and the Studio `/requests` page shows a criterion's findings; the beat row (`.pravrudhi/heartbeat.jsonl`) records `findings_read` for a dispatch so the met-rate with and without prior findings can be compared from existing rows; tests

requests.text: The product repository AxisMeru/pravrudhi-app (ADR-0049) has no development loop of its own: build mode dispatches under the `selfbuild` sandbox policy whose validate command is the engine's (`uv run ruff check src tests && uv run pytest -q tests`, `integrate.BUILD_VALIDATE`), so a heartbeat run in a JavaScript/TypeScript repository would validate nothing it built. Let a root declare its own validate command and allowed prefixes, so `pravrudhi init` + a heartbeat timer in ~/projects/pravrudhi-app gives the product the same loop the studio has (frontend: `npx tsc --noEmit && npx eslint . && npm test && npm run build`; desktop: `node --test test/`).

roster.note: Costs nothing and, on the evidence so far, does little: it produced no change at all on two tasks a hosted agent completed in minutes. Serving text and driving an agentic tool-calling loop are different capabilities. Restored to the mechanical tier only, and declared behind sonnet, so it is reached solely when the paid route is cooling. Last resort, not a peer.

The same Lite Plan, its cheap high-throughput model. Added 2026-09-08 after the plan's one-week quota was exhausted inside a day. The cause was not one expensive call: qwen3.8-max, the vendor's FLAGSHIP, was the declared first choice at both mechanical and standard, driving agent loops whose steps cost about 20,000 tokens each (one measured step of a trivial task: 20,419 total, 19,584 read from cache), dispatched hourly. Mechanical work is what a fast cheap model is for. The two share one quota, so this buys no capacity; it lowers the burn rate for the work that never needed the flagship, which is most of it. Admitted at mechanical only -- the same tier the plan's other model earned on one verified tool call -- because a cheaper model is not thereby a better one.

Alibaba's Lite Plan flagship, on a plan-exclusive endpoint with its own key file and a credit budget rather than a free-tier token cap. Verified live on 2026-09-07: given a file and a read tool it called the tool and returned the right answer, exit 0 in 8.6s. Admitted at the two tiers the free-tier loop was admitted at, on the same evidence and the same reasoning -- one verified tool call says the loop runs, not that it does design or critical work well. It is declared ahead of the free-tier loop because it is cheaper and the vendor's stronger model, and it rises further only on its measured record here.

A hosted free-tier model with no CLI: it cannot drive a tool-calling loop, only answer once with a JSON payload of whole-file contents. It is the SENTINEL. Permitted at every tier but declared last everywhere above mechanical, so the router reaches it only when every paid route at that tier is cooling down from a usage limit. A single-shot writer is a poor substitute for an agent loop and a far better one than a stopped loop, which is what the operator asked for on 2026-09-06: the system must run unattended when the paid accounts are spent. It stays because the loop above it is a different route and can also be spent.

Out of the tiers since 2026-09-08: the free tier's coding quota is spent. Asked to do work it answers "The free quota has been exhausted", observed through the agent rather than assumed, so it is a route the swarm can no longer choose. The subscribed Lite Plan (qwen-lite-max) is the Alibaba seat that works and is first at both tiers it serves. Kept here rather than deleted because the quota resets and the record of what it did is worth keeping. Qwen driving a real tool loop through OpenCode against DashScope Singapore. Verified live on 2026-09-07: given a file and a read tool it called the tool and returned the right answer, exit 0 in 8.1s at zero cost. An earlier attempt from inside a sandboxed agent failed at OpenCode's own log file before reaching DashScope, which is a property of nesting one agent inside another's sandbox and not of this route; agents/ALIBABA_LOOP.md keeps that transcript. Admitted at mechanical and standard because one verified tool call is evidence the loop runs, not evidence it does design or critical work well. It rises through the same measured outcomes as every other route, or it does not rise.

Kept in the table so the router can be told to try it again deliberately.
